html:
The main problem of interest here is to solve a square linear system, which in matrix form reads

Ax=b,A∈RN×N.\displaystyle Ax=b,\quad A\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}.Ax=b,A∈RN×N.

The type of algorithm that operating directly on the matrix A {A}A belongs to the family of direct methods. The simple Gaussian elimination (LU decomposition) is one of this kind, and can be used to solve such a system in O(N3) {O(N^{3})}O(N3) time, yielding an exact solution. But that is not always preferable, because it is typically time and power consuming when the matrix A {A}A is too large and no structural information of A {A}A is used in the algorithm. Various improvements of computation complexity in direct methods are possible, but will be a research topic. Here, we will take a look at some simple indirect methods, or iterative methods, which try to avoid computation with A {A}A as much as possible.

Generally speaking, one instead deals with the equivalent system

Mx=(M−A)x+b\displaystyle Mx=(M-A)x+bMx=(M−A)x+b

where M {M}M has to be designed based on A {A}A. This can be seen as a splitting of A {A}A

A=M+(A−M).\displaystyle A=M+(A-M).A=M+(A−M).

And then we will take the fixed point iteration

Mxk+1=(M−A)xk+b\displaystyle Mx^{k+1}=(M-A)x^{k}+bMxk+1=(M−A)xk+b

since if x∗=A−1b {x^{*}=A^{-1}b}x∗=A−1b, it is a fixed point of the above iteration

Mx∗=(M−A)x∗+b.\displaystyle Mx^{*}=(M-A)x^{*}+b.Mx∗=(M−A)x∗+b.

Whether this iteration converges or not needs to be analysed. To do this, we consider the discrepancy of x∗ {x^{*}}x∗ from the k {k}k-th iteration

ek+1=x∗−xk+1=M−1(M−A)(x∗−xk)=M−1(M−A)ek=:Bek.\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl} e^{k+1} & = & x^{*}-x^{k+1}\\ & = & M^{-1}(M-A)(x^{*}-x^{k})\\ & = & M^{-1}(M-A)e^{k}\\ & =: & Be^{k}. \end{array}ek+1​====:​x∗−xk+1M−1(M−A)(x∗−xk)M−1(M−A)ekBek.​

This means the convergence is controled by the powers of the error matrix B {B}B, and the iteration converges if and only if

Bn→0 as n→∞.\displaystyle B^{n}\rightarrow0\text{ as }n\rightarrow\infty.Bn→0 as n→∞.

Exercise 1 Show that Bn→0 {B^{n}\rightarrow0}Bn→0 if and only if every eigenvalue λi {\lambda_{i}}λi​ of B{B}B has modulus strictly less than one, i.e.

∣λi∣<1∀i.\displaystyle |\lambda_{i}|<1\quad\forall i.∣λi​∣<1∀i.

(Hint: use the Jordan normal form of B {B}B.) The largest eigenvalue in modulus governs the rate of convergence, which is called the spectral radius, or L2L^2L2 operator norm of the matrix B {B}B.

There are several criteria on what a "good'' M {M}M should be:

  • M {M}M is easy to invert.
  • M−A {M-A}M−A is easy to compute.
  • The matrix B:=M−1(M−A) {B:=M^{-1}(M-A)}B:=M−1(M−A) has spectral radius stricly less than one.

Below the fold let us look at some simple concrete choices of M {M}M. For this purpose we write

A=L+D+U\displaystyle A=L+D+UA=L+D+U

where L,D,U {L,D,U}L,D,U are the strict lower triangular part, diagonal part and strict upper triangular part of A {A}A respectively.

1.1. The Jacobi iteration

This unfortunately is a rather uninformative name. We take

M=D.\displaystyle M=D.M=D.

Hence in order for M {M}M to be invertible, the diagonal part of A {A}A must be non-zero. We will see that a sufficient condition for the iteration to converge is a condition on the diagonal part of A {A}A.

Let us take a small concrete example to see what is going on. Take

A=[2−1−12].\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1\\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}.A=[2−1​−12​].

One Jacobi iteration looks like the following

[22][x01x11]=[11][x00x10]+b.\displaystyle \begin{bmatrix}2\\ & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_{0}^{1}\\ x_{1}^{1} \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} & 1\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_{0}^{0}\\ x_{1}^{0} \end{bmatrix}+b.[2​2​][x01​x11​​]=[1​1][x00​x10​​]+b.

Note that one has to store the entire x0 {x^{0}}x0 in order to compute x1 {x^{1}}x1. This is what happens in general, since M−A {M-A}M−A is usually not triangular.

The error matrix is

B=D−1(D−A),\displaystyle B=D^{-1}(D-A),B=D−1(D−A),

where we recognize D−A {D-A}D−A is the negative non-diagonal part of A {A}A. So B {B}B is the negative non-diagonal part of A {A}A, with each row divided by the corresponding diagonal entry, which was assumed to be non-zero. The larger the diagonal entries are, the closer to zero B {B}B becomes. To make this condition precise, we need the following useful fact.

Exercise 2 (Gershgorin disk) Let A=(aij)∈RN×N {A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}}A=(aij​)∈RN×N. Then each eigenvalue of A {A}A (which can be complex) lies within at least one of the closed disks {z:∣z−aii∣≤Ri} {\{z:|z-a_{ii}|\leq R_{i}\}}{z:∣z−aii​∣≤Ri​} in C {\mathbb{C}}C, where the radius Ri {R_{i}}Ri​ is defined by

Ri=∑j≠i∣aij∣.\displaystyle R_{i}=\sum_{j\neq i}|a_{ij}|.Ri​=j=i∑​∣aij​∣.

Exercise 3 What are the Gershgorin disks of the matrix B {B}B in the Jacobi iteration? Hence show that Jacobi iteration is convergent if the matrix A {A}A is strictly diagonal dominant (SDD), i.e.

∣aii∣>∑j≠i∣aij∣.\displaystyle |a_{ii}|>\sum_{j\neq i}|a_{ij}|.∣aii​∣>j=i∑​∣aij​∣.

Exercise 4 Show that a SDD matrix is invertible.

1.2. The Gauss-Seidel iteration

Again unfortunately this name is rather uninformative. I would rather call it method of successive displacement, for reason to be clear in a moment. We take

M=D+U  or  M=D+L.\displaystyle M=D+U\:\text{ or }\:M=D+L.M=D+U or M=D+L.

Now since M {M}M is triangular, its eigenvalues lie on the diagonal. Hence in order for M {M}M to be invertible, the diagonal of A {A}A must be nonzero. The same SDD condition is also sufficient for the Gauss-Seidel to converge.

We take the same example to illustrate what is going on. With

A=[2−1−12],M=[2−12]\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1\\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix},\quad M=\begin{bmatrix}2\\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}A=[2−1​−12​],M=[2−1​2​]

one Gauss-Seidel iteration looks like the following

[2−12][x01x11]=[1][x00x10]+b.\displaystyle \begin{bmatrix}2\\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_{0}^{1}\\ x_{1}^{1} \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} & 1\\ \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_{0}^{0}\\ x_{1}^{0} \end{bmatrix}+b.[2−1​2​][x01​x11​​]=[​1​][x00​x10​​]+b.

Note that to obtain x11 {x_{1}^{1}}x11​, one needs x01 {x_{0}^{1}}x01​ and x10 {x_{1}^{0}}x10​ but not x00 {x_{0}^{0}}x00​, due to our choice that M {M}M is the lower triangular part of A {A}A, and cpnsequently M−A {M-A}M−A is strictly upper triangular. So, instead of storing the entire x0 {x^{0}}x0 before x1 {x^{1}}x1 is obtained, one can replace the entry x00 {x_{0}^{0}}x00​ with the computed x01 {x_{0}^{1}}x01​ immediately, hence saving half of the storage.

Exercise 5 Check the case M=D+U {M=D+U}M=D+U using the above 2×2 {2\times2}2×2 example.

The SDD condition still guarantees the convergence here. Assume M {M}M is taken to be the lower triangular part (the other case is similar). Now consider the eigenvlaues λ {\lambda}λ of

B=M−1(M−A)=−M−1U.\displaystyle B=M^{-1}(M-A)=-M^{-1}U.B=M−1(M−A)=−M−1U.

We have

ker⁡(−M−1U−λI)≠{0}.\displaystyle \ker(-M^{-1}U-\lambda I)\neq\{0\}.ker(−M−1U−λI)={0}.

Since M {M}M is invertible, this implies

ker⁡(U+λM)≠{0}.\displaystyle \ker(U+\lambda M)\neq\{0\}.ker(U+λM)={0}.

Note that U+λM=U+λD+λL {U+\lambda M=U+\lambda D+\lambda L}U+λM=U+λD+λL. If A {A}A is SDD, then U+λD+λL {U+\lambda D+\lambda L}U+λD+λL is SDD only if ∣λ∣≥1 {|\lambda|\geq1}∣λ∣≥1. But if ∣λ∣≥1 {|\lambda|\geq1}∣λ∣≥1, U+λD+λL {U+\lambda D+\lambda L}U+λD+λL is invertible, by Exercise 4. This shows that eigenvalues of B {B}B in modulus cannot be greater than 1 {1}1 if A {A}A is SDD. This guarantees the convergence by Exercise 1.

Another sufficient condition for convergence. Besides the SDD conditions, we also have

Theorem 1

*- The Gauss-Seidel iteration converges if A {A}A is symmetric and positive definite.

  • The Jacobi iteration converges if both A {A}A and 2D−A {2D-A}2D−A are symmetric positive definite.*

These are immediate consequences of

Theorem 2 (Householder-John) If A,B∈RN×N {A,B\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}}A,B∈RN×N and both A {A}A and A−B−BT {A-B-B^{T}}A−B−BT are symmetric positive definite, then the spectral radius of (A−B)−1B {(A-B)^{-1}B}(A−B)−1B is stricly less than one.

Proof: Let λ {\lambda}λ,v≠0 {v\neq0}v=0 be an eigenvalue-eigenvector pair of −(A−B)−1B {-(A-B)^{-1}B}−(A−B)−1B, which may well be complex. Then

−Bv=λ(A−B)v.\displaystyle -Bv=\lambda(A-B)v.−Bv=λ(A−B)v.

Hence λ≠1 {\lambda\neq1}λ=1 since A {A}A is invertible. Multiplying both sides by vˉT {\bar{v}^{T}}vˉT, we obtain

−vˉTBv=λvˉTAv+λvˉTBv.\displaystyle -\bar{v}^{T}Bv=\lambda\bar{v}^{T}Av+\lambda\bar{v}^{T}Bv.−vˉTBv=λvˉTAv+λvˉTBv.

Thus

vˉTBv=λλ−1vˉTAv.\displaystyle \bar{v}^{T}Bv=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-1}\bar{v}^{T}Av.vˉTBv=λ−1λ​vˉTAv.

Now one easily check that the symmetric positive definiteness of a matrix M {M}M implies

xˉTMx>0,∀x∈CN.\displaystyle \bar{x}^{T}Mx>0\quad,\forall x\in\mathbb{C}^{N}.xˉTMx>0,∀x∈CN.

Also,

vˉTBTv=(vˉTBv)∗=λˉλˉ−1vˉTA∗v=λˉλˉ−1vˉTAv.\displaystyle \bar{v}^{T}B^{T}v=\left(\bar{v}^{T}Bv\right)^{*}=\frac{\bar{\lambda}}{\bar{\lambda}-1}\bar{v}^{T}A^{*}v=\frac{\bar{\lambda}}{\bar{\lambda}-1}\bar{v}^{T}Av.vˉTBTv=(vˉTBv)∗=λˉ−1λˉ​vˉTA∗v=λˉ−1λˉ​vˉTAv.

Apply the above observations to M=A−B−BT {M=A-B-B^{T}}M=A−B−BT and M=A {M=A}M=A, with x=v {x=v}x=v, we get

0<vˉT(A−B−BT)v=vˉTAv−λλ−1vˉTAv−λˉλˉ−1vˉTAv=1−∣λ∣2∣1−λ∣2vˉTAv\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl} 0 & < & \bar{v}^{T}(A-B-B^{T})v\\ & = & \bar{v}^{T}Av-\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-1}\bar{v}^{T}Av-\frac{\bar{\lambda}}{\bar{\lambda}-1}\bar{v}^{T}Av\\ & = & \frac{1-|\lambda|^{2}}{|1-\lambda|^{2}}\bar{v}^{T}Av \end{array}0​<==​vˉT(A−B−BT)vvˉTAv−λ−1λ​vˉTAv−λˉ−1λˉ​vˉTAv∣1−λ∣21−∣λ∣2​vˉTAv​

and

We deduce that ∣λ∣<1 {|\lambda|<1}∣λ∣<1. □ \Box□
